propositions.text: Determine if Alberta's Personal Information Protection Act unjustifiably limits union's freedom of expression during lawful strike.
propositions.quote: This appeal requires the Court to determine whether Alberta’s Personal Information Protection Act unjustifiably limits a union’s right to freedom of expression in the context of a lawful strike.

propositions.text: Whether the Act balances individuals' control over personal information and union's freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: At issue is whether the Act achieves a constitutionally acceptable balance between the interests of individuals in controlling the collection, use and disclosure of their personal information and a union’s freedom of expression.

paragraphs.summary: The Court must decide if Alberta's Act unjustifiably limits union expression and balances privacy with union rights.

propositions.text: Union recorded and photographed individuals crossing picketline during labour dispute.
propositions.quote: The dispute in this case arose when the United Food and Commercial Workers, Local 401 recorded and photographed individuals crossing its picketline for use in its labour dispute.

propositions.text: Individuals complained to Privacy Commissioner that Union's activities contravened PIPA.
propositions.quote: Several individuals whose images were captured complained to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta that the Union’s activities contravened the Personal Information Protection Act

propositions.text: Individuals were successful, prompting judicial review application alleging Charter infringement.
propositions.quote: Those individuals were successful, prompting an application for judicial review on the basis that the legislation infringed the Union’s right to freedom of expression under s. 2 (b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and that this infringement was not justified under s. 1 .

paragraphs.summary: Union recorded picketline; individuals complained under PIPA; judicial review applied alleging Charter breach.

propositions.text: Legislation violates s. 2(b) because its impact on freedom of expression is disproportionate and not justified under s.1.
propositions.quote: In our view, the legislation violates s. 2 (b) because its impact on freedom of expression in the labour context is disproportionate and the infringement is not justified under s. 1 .

paragraphs.summary: Court finds legislation violates freedom of expression and is not justified under s.1.

propositions.text: Union represented employees at Palace Casino during 305-day lawful strike and videotaped picketline.
propositions.quote: The Union represents employees at the Palace Casino at West Edmonton Mall in Alberta. In 2006, during a lawful strike which lasted 305 days, both the Union and a security company hired by the employer video-taped and photographed the picketline near the main entrance to the Casino.

propositions.text: Union posted signs warning images might be placed on website www.casinoscabs.ca.
propositions.quote: The Union posted signs in the area of the picketing stating that images of persons crossing the picketline might be placed on a website called www.casinoscabs.ca.

paragraphs.summary: Union videotaped picketline during lawful strike and posted signs about image use on website.

propositions.text: Several individuals complained to Privacy Commissioner about being recorded crossing picketline.
propositions.quote: Several individuals who were recorded crossing the picketline filed complaints with the Alberta Information and Privacy Commissioner under PIPA.

propositions.text: Casino Vice-President complained about photos used on posters and newsletters with humorous captions.
propositions.quote: The Vice-President of the Casino complained that he was photographed or video-taped and that two pictures of him were used on a poster displayed at the picketline with the text: “This is [x’s] Police Mugshot.” Images of his head were also used in union newsletters and strike leaflets with captions intended to be humorous.

propositions.text: Other complainants testified about being recorded near Casino entrance; no recordings placed on website.
propositions.quote: Another complainant, a member of the public, testified that cameras were trained on the entrance to the Casino where he would regularly meet friends. A third complainant testified that she had been photographed and video-taped while working near the Casino entrance. No recordings of the complainants were placed on the website.

paragraphs.summary: Individuals complained about being recorded crossing picketline; some images used in posters and newsletters.

propositions.text: Commissioner appointed Adjudicator who lacked jurisdiction to decide constitutional questions.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner appointed an Adjudicator to decide whether the Union, in collecting, using and disclosing personal information about individuals without their consent had contravened PIPA. In Alberta, the Administrative Procedures and Jurisdiction Act... prevent the Commissioner from deciding questions of constitutional law.

propositions.text: Adjudicator accepted Union's evidence that videotaping picketlines is common practice for various expressive and protective purposes.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator accepted the Union’s evidence that it is common practice in Alberta for both employers and unions to video-tape and photograph picketlines and that the Union did so for the following reasons: • informing the public about the strike...

propositions.text: Adjudicator concluded Union's collection, use and disclosure was for expressive purpose to dissuade crossing picketline.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator concluded that the Union’s collection, use and disclosure of private information was for an expressive purpose. As she put it, “one of the primary purposes of the Union’s information collection was to dissuade people from crossing the picket line”: para. 51.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found no PIPA provision authorizing collection for dissuading crossing picketline.
propositions.quote: She also concluded that she was not aware of, and had not been referred to, any provisions of PIPA that would authorize collection, use and disclosure of personal information for that purpose: para. 67.

propositions.text: Adjudicator rejected Union's claim of journalistic exemption as activities aimed at resolving labour dispute.
propositions.quote: She rejected the Union’s claim that it was covered by the “journalistic purposes” exemption because its activities were also aimed at resolving the labour dispute in its favour.

propositions.text: Adjudicator accepted investigation or legal proceeding exemption but insufficient to exempt other purposes.
propositions.quote: The Union’s ancillary argument — that the collection, use and disclosure of personal information was authorized under another exemption — a possible investigation or legal proceeding — was accepted, but was not sufficient to exempt the Union’s activity from PIPA for any other purpose.

propositions.text: Union ordered to stop collecting personal information for any other purpose.
propositions.quote: The Union was ordered to stop collecting the personal information for any

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found Union's videotaping was expressive but not authorized by PIPA exemptions; ordered to stop collecting info.

propositions.text: Union argued PIPA provisions infringe s. 2(b) Charter right to freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: On judicial review, the Union argued that the provisions of PIPA that prevent it from collecting, using and disclosing personal information obtained from its lawful picketline infringed s. 2 (b) of the Charter

propositions.text: Chambers judge found Union's activity had expressive content and was protected by s. 2(b).
propositions.quote: The chambers judge found that the Union’s activity had expressive content and that there was no reason to exclude it from the protection of s. 2 (b).

propositions.text: Chambers judge found PIPA directly limited Union's freedom of expression by preventing collection and use of personal info.
propositions.quote: She found that PIPA, as interpreted by the Adjudicator, directly limited the Union’s freedom of expression by preventing the Union from collecting, using, and disclosing personal information obtained about individuals while they were in public view.

propositions.text: Chambers judge concluded breach could not be justified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: She also concluded that the breach could not be justified under s. 1 .

paragraphs.summary: Union argued PIPA infringed Charter; chambers judge agreed and found breach not justified.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found issue was justifiability of restraining expression in labour relations.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal was of the view that the real issue in the case was whether it was justifiable to restrain expression in support of labour relations and collective bargaining activities

propositions.text: Court of Appeal concluded PIPA was overbroad and privacy interest minor as complainants were in public with notice.
propositions.quote: It concluded that PIPA was overbroad. The privacy interest at stake was minor since the complainants were in a public place, crossing a picketline, and had notice that images were being collected.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal balanced workers' collective bargaining rights and union communication rights against privacy.
propositions.quote: On the other side of the balance was the right of workers to engage in collective bargaining and of the Union to communicate with the public: para. 74.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed with chambers judge that s. 2(b) breach existed and was not saved under s. 1; granted constitutional exemption.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal agreed with the chambers judge that there was a breach of s. 2 (b) that could not be saved under s. 1 and it therefore granted the Union a constitutional exemption from the application of PIPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found PIPA overbroad, privacy interest minor, breach of s.2(b) not justified, granted exemption.

propositions.text: Constitutional questions: Does PIPA violate s. 2(b) restricting union's collection/use/disclosure during lawful strike?
propositions.quote: Do the Personal Information Protection Act... violate s. 2 (b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms insofar as they restrict a union’s ability to collect, use or disclose personal information during the course of a lawful strike?

propositions.text: If so, is the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
propositions.quote: If so, is the infringement a reasonable limit prescribed by law, which can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under s. 1 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ?

paragraphs.summary: Court frames constitutional questions on PIPA's violation of s.2(b) and justification under s.1.

propositions.text: PIPA limits expressive activity protected by s. 2(b).
propositions.quote: there can be no doubt, in our view, that PIPA limits expressive activity that is so protected.

propositions.text: Reviewing judge and Court of Appeal recognized Union's collection/use/disclosure of personal info during lawful strike is inherently expressive.
propositions.quote: The reviewing judge and the Court of Appeal both recognized that the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by the Union in the context of picketing during a lawful strike is inherently expressive.

propositions.text: Case arises in factual context before Adjudicator but challenge is to PIPA as a whole.
propositions.quote: This case arises in the specific factual context that was before the Adjudicator, but the challenge is to PIPA as a whole.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees PIPA limits protected expressive activity; challenge is to PIPA generally.

propositions.text: Freedom of expression under s. 2(b) is clearly engaged by Union's recording of picketline.
propositions.quote: As the parties conceded, freedom of expression under s. 2 (b) is clearly engaged by the Union’s activities.

propositions.text: Adjudicator recognized primary purpose of Union's collection was to dissuade crossing picketline.
propositions.quote: One of the primary purposes for the Union’s collection of personal information was, as the Adjudicator recognized, to dissuade people from crossing the picketline: para. 51;

propositions.text: Recording conduct related to picketing is expressive activity aimed at persuasion and informing public.
propositions.quote: Recording conduct related to picketing and, in particular, recording a lawful picketline and any individuals who crossed it, is expressive activity: its purpose was to persuade individuals to support the Union.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Union's recording picketline is expressive activity protected by s.2(b).

propositions.text: Reviewing PIPA's provisions helps understand how it limits Union's expressive activities.
propositions.quote: To understand how PIPA limited the Union’s expressive activities, it is helpful to review the legislation in some detail.

paragraphs.summary: Court will review PIPA provisions to understand limits on Union's expression.

propositions.text: Alberta's PIPA inspired by federal PIPEDA, part of international movement for personal information control.
propositions.quote: Alberta’s PIPA was inspired by the federal Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act... Both pieces of legislation are part of an international movement towards giving individuals better control over their personal information

propositions.text: PIPEDA applies to private sector commercial activities but not if province has comparable protection like PIPA.
propositions.quote: PIPEDA generally applies to private sector organizations engaged in commercial activities in any province. It does not apply, however, if the Governor in Council determines that there is comparable protection in place in the province, as is the case with respect to PIPA in Alberta

paragraphs.summary: PIPA inspired by PIPEDA, part of global trend to enhance personal information control.

propositions.text: PIPA's purpose is to govern collection, use and disclosure of personal information balancing individual rights and organizational needs.
propositions.quote: PIPA’s purpose is explicitly set out in s. 3, which states that it is to govern the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by organizations in a manner that recognizes both the right of an individual to have his or her personal information protected and the need of organizations to collect, use or disclose personal information for purposes that are reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: PIPA aims to balance individual privacy rights with organizations' reasonable use of personal information.

propositions.text: PIPA's scope broader than PIPEDA; applies beyond commercial purposes to all organizations and personal information.
propositions.quote: Unlike PIPEDA, PIPA’s limitations on the collection, use and disclosure of personal information are not restricted to those activities undertaken for commercial purposes. Instead, PIPA establishes a general rule that organizations cannot collect, use or disclose personal information without consent

propositions.text: PIPA defines 'organization' broadly including unions; 'personal information' includes publicly known info.
propositions.quote: The term “organization” includes a corporation, an unincorporated association, a trade union... The term “personal information” is defined broadly to mean “information about an identifiable individual”... personal information does not lose its character as personal information if the information is widely or publicly known

paragraphs.summary: PIPA broadly applies to all organizations including unions and covers all personal information, even public.

propositions.text: PIPA has exemptions: excludes individuals acting personally, non-profits unless commercial, artistic/literary, journalistic, and some investigation/legal exceptions.
propositions.quote: The breadth of PIPA is mitigated by a series of exemptions... excludes from its application individuals acting in a “personal or domestic capacity”... does not apply to a non-profit unless commercial... artistic or literary purposes... journalistic purposes... exceptions for investigation or legal proceeding

propositions.text: Adjudicator found none of these exemptions applied to Union's collection for labour dispute purposes.
propositions.quote: Given the Adjudicator’s finding that none of these exemptions applied to allow the Union to collect, use and disclose personal information for the purpose of advancing its interests in a labour dispute

paragraphs.summary: PIPA has exemptions but none applied to Union's collection for labour dispute purposes.

propositions.text: PIPA restricts freedom of expression as none of the exemptions apply to Union's activities.
propositions.quote: we conclude without difficulty that it restricts freedom of expression.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes PIPA restricts Union's freedom of expression.

propositions.text: S.1 analysis: whether PIPA serves pressing and substantial objective and is justified proportionately.
propositions.quote: At this stage, we must determine whether PIPA serves a pressing and substantial objective and, if so, whether its provisions are rationally connected to that objective, whether it impairs the right to freedom of expression no more than is necessary, and whether its effects are proportionate to the government’s objective.

propositions.text: PIPA is rationally connected to pressing objective but its broad limits on expression are disproportionate and not justified.
propositions.quote: While PIPA is rationally connected to a pressing and substantial objective, its broad limitations on freedom of expression are not demonstrably justified because its limitations on expression are disproportionate to the benefits the legislation seeks to promote.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PIPA's objective pressing and rational but its broad limits on expression disproportionate and unjustified.

propositions.text: PIPA's purpose is to protect individual control over personal information, linked to autonomy, dignity and privacy.
propositions.quote: The purpose of PIPA is explicitly set out in s. 3... The focus is on providing an individual with some measure of control over his or her personal information... The ability of individuals to control their personal information is intimately connected to their individual autonomy, dignity and privacy.

propositions.text: Privacy legislation is quasi-constitutional due to fundamental role of privacy in democracy.
propositions.quote: legislation which aims to protect control over personal information should be characterized as “quasi-constitutional” because of the fundamental role privacy plays in the preservation of a free and democratic society

paragraphs.summary: PIPA protects individual control over personal info, a fundamental democratic value; privacy laws are quasi-constitutional.

propositions.text: PIPA's objective is significant in modern context of technology enabling extensive personal info collection and use.
propositions.quote: PIPA’s objective is increasingly significant in the modern context, where new technologies give organizations an almost unlimited capacity to collect personal information, analyze it, use it and communicate it to others for their own purposes.

propositions.text: PIPA is rationally connected to objective but its broad restrictions are disproportionate to benefits and unjustified.
propositions.quote: There is also no serious question that PIPA is rationally connected to this important objective... these broad restrictions are not justified because they are disproportionate to the benefits the legislation seeks to promote.

propositions.text: Charter infringement is too high a price for the law's benefit if disproportionate.
propositions.quote: “the Charter infringement is too high a price to pay for the benefit of the law”: Peter W. Hogg, Constitutional Law of Canada (5th ed. Supp.), vol. 2, at p. 38-43.

paragraphs.summary: PIPA's objective is important and rational but broad restrictions are disproportionate; infringement too high a price.

propositions.text: PIPA aims to enhance individual control over personal information by restricting collection, use and disclosure without consent.
propositions.quote: PIPA seeks to enhance an individual’s control over his or her personal information by restricting who can collect, use and disclose personal information without that individual’s consent

propositions.text: PIPA reflects recognition that many private sector actors now access and use personal information.
propositions.quote: PIPA and legislation like it reflect an emerging recognition that the list of those who may access and use personal information has expanded dramatically and now includes many private sector actors.

propositions.text: Informational privacy's foundational principle is that all information about a person is fundamentally theirs to control.
propositions.quote: informational privacy, the foundational principle of which is that “all information about a person is in a fundamental way his own, for him to communicate or retain . . . as he sees fit”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains PIPA's goal to enhance individual control over personal information and its foundational privacy principle.

propositions.text: PIPA is quasi-constitutional in nature due to its role in safeguarding informational privacy.
propositions.quote: Insofar as PIPA seeks to safeguard informational privacy, it is “quasi-constitutional” in nature

propositions.text: Protection of privacy is crucial in a vibrant democracy.
propositions.quote: The importance of the protection of privacy in a vibrant democracy cannot be overstated

propositions.text: Privacy invasions inhibit individuality and conformity harms democracy.
propositions.quote: If invasions of privacy inhibit individuality and produce conformity, democracy itself suffers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states PIPA's quasi-constitutional nature and the vital role of privacy protection in democracy.

propositions.text: PIPA aims to prevent harm from permanent storage or unlimited dissemination of personal information without consent.
propositions.quote: PIPA also seeks to avoid the potential harm that flows from the permanent storage or unlimited dissemination of personal information through the Internet or other forms of technology without an individual’s consent.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes PIPA's goal to prevent harm from uncontrolled dissemination of personal information.

propositions.text: PIPA's objective of individual control over personal information is linked to autonomy, dignity, and privacy.
propositions.quote: the objective of providing an individual with some measure of control over his or her personal information is intimately connected to individual autonomy, dignity and privacy

paragraphs.summary: The court links PIPA's control objective to significant social values like autonomy and dignity.

propositions.text: PIPA's restrictions are disproportionate to its benefits because it limits personal information use without regard to context.
propositions.quote: PIPA limits the collection, use and disclosure of personal information other than with consent without regard for the nature of the personal information, the purpose for which it is collected, used or disclosed, and the situational context

propositions.text: The Adjudicator found PIPA does not accommodate unions' expressive purposes during lawful strikes.
propositions.quote: As the Adjudicator recognized in her decision, PIPA does not provide any way to accommodate the expressive purposes of unions engaged in lawful strikes.

propositions.text: PIPA lacks mechanisms to balance union freedom of expression with privacy interests.
propositions.quote: the Act does not include any mechanisms by which a union’s constitutional right to freedom of expression may be balanced with the interests protected by the legislation.

propositions.text: The Commissioner’s counsel conceded PIPA generally prohibits union use of personal information without consent for collective bargaining.
propositions.quote: As counsel for the Commissioner conceded during oral submissions, PIPA contains a general prohibition of the Union’s use of personal information (absent consent or deemed consent) to further its collective bargaining objectives.

propositions.text: PIPA deems virtually all personal information protected regardless of context.
propositions.quote: PIPA deems virtually all personal information to be protected regardless of context.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PIPA's broad restrictions disproportionate and lacking balance for union expression during strikes.

propositions.text: In this case, personal information was collected at a public demonstration and was publicly observable.
propositions.quote: The personal information was collected by the Union at an open political demonstration where it was readily and publicly observable.

propositions.text: Individuals crossing the picketline would reasonably expect their image could be recorded and disseminated by others.
propositions.quote: Those crossing the picketline would reasonably expect that their image could be caught and disseminated by others such as journalists, for example.

propositions.text: The personal information collected was limited to images and did not reveal intimate biographical details.
propositions.quote: the personal information collected, used and disclosed by the Union was limited to images of individuals crossing a picketline and did not include intimate biographical details.

propositions.text: No intimate lifestyle or personal choice details were revealed.
propositions.quote: No intimate details of the lifestyle or personal choices of the individuals were revealed.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the personal information collected was publicly observable images without intimate details.

propositions.text: Appearing in public does not mean forfeiting control over personal information exposed.
propositions.quote: by appearing in public, an individual does not automatically forfeit his or her interest in retaining control over the personal information which is thereby exposed.

propositions.text: Technology enables easy recording, wide distribution, and indefinite storage of personal information.
propositions.quote: developments in technology that make it possible for personal information to be recorded with ease, distributed to an almost infinite audience, and stored indefinitely.

propositions.text: PIPA's restrictions in this case impede expression on significant public interest matters.
propositions.quote: PIPA’s restrictions operate in the context of a case like this one to impede the formulation and expression of views on matters of significant public interest and importance.

paragraphs.summary: The court states public appearance doesn't forfeit privacy, but PIPA restricts expression on important public issues.

propositions.text: PIPA prohibits collection, use, or disclosure of personal information for legitimate expressive labour relations purposes.
propositions.quote: PIPA prohibits the collection, use, or disclosure of personal information for many legitimate, expressive purposes related to labour relations.

propositions.text: These expressive purposes include safety, persuading public, and public debate on labour conditions.
propositions.quote: These purposes include ensuring the safety of union members, attempting to persuade the public not to do business with an employer and bringing debate on the labour conditions with an employer into the public realm.

propositions.text: These objectives are core protected expressive activity under s. 2(b) of the Charter.
propositions.quote: These objectives are at the core of protected expressive activity under s. 2 (b).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PIPA restricts core expressive activities protected by the Charter in labour relations.

propositions.text: The Court has recognized freedom of expression's fundamental importance in labour disputes.
propositions.quote: This Court has long recognized the fundamental importance of freedom of expression in the context of labour disputes

propositions.text: Freedom of expression is essential in labour relations for employees.
propositions.quote: For employees, freedom of expression becomes not only an important but an essential component of labour relations

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent recognizing freedom of expression as essential in labour disputes.

propositions.text: Expressive activity in labour relates to Charter s. 2(d) right to associate for workplace goals.
propositions.quote: Expressive activity in the labour context is directly related to the Charter protected right of workers to associate to further common workplace goals under s. 2 (d) of the Charter

propositions.text: ILO states freedom of association and collective bargaining depend on civil liberties including freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: The exercise of freedom of association and collective bargaining is dependent on the maintenance of fundamental civil liberties, in particular, . . . freedom of opinion and expression

paragraphs.summary: The court notes labour expression relates to Charter association rights and ILO's recognition of civil liberties.

propositions.text: Employment and workplace conditions affect identity and self-worth.
propositions.quote: A person’s employment and the conditions of their workplace can inform their identity, emotional health, and sense of self-worth

propositions.text: Free expression on workplace issues contributes to self-understanding and influence over life.
propositions.quote: free expression on these issues therefore “contributes to self-understanding, as well as to the ability to influence one’s working and non-working life”

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that free expression on workplace issues supports identity and life influence.

propositions.text: Free expression helps redress imbalance between employer power and worker vulnerability.
propositions.quote: Free expression in the labour context can also play a significant role in redressing or alleviating the presumptive imbalance between the employer’s economic power and the relative vulnerability of the individual worker

propositions.text: Unions use expressive activities to promote interests and persuade employers during disputes.
propositions.quote: It is through their expressive activities that unions are able to articulate and promote their common interests, and, in the event of a labour dispute, to attempt to persuade the employer.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains free expression helps balance employer-worker power and supports union advocacy.

propositions.text: Free expression by unions brings labour issues into public debate.
propositions.quote: the free flow of expression by unions and their members during a labour dispute plays an important role in bringing issues relating to labour conditions into the public arena for discussion and debate

propositions.text: Free expression allows unions to frame collective bargaining as public, not just economic, disputes.
propositions.quote: free expression provides “an avenue for unions to promote collective bargaining issues as public ones to be played out in civic society, rather than being confined to a narrow realm of individualized economic disputes”

paragraphs.summary: The court cites that union free expression promotes public discussion of labour issues beyond economic disputes.

propositions.text: Since WWII, Canadian government recognizes unions' role in economy and society.
propositions.quote: Since the Second World War, the Canadian government has recognized that unions have a role to play in the Canadian economy and society more broadly

propositions.text: Workers have right to associate and bargain collectively; economic sanctions may be legitimate in disputes.
propositions.quote: workers have the right to associate and bargain collectively and that when collective bargaining breaks down, unions and employers may, in certain circumstances, legitimately exert economic sanctions

paragraphs.summary: The court notes historical recognition of unions' societal role and collective bargaining rights.

propositions.text: Picketing is a crucial form of expression with strong historical roots in Canadian unions.
propositions.quote: picketlines have been used by Canadian unions to exert economic pressure and bargain with employers for over a century

propositions.text: Picketing is a key economic sanction in collective bargaining, driving negotiations and settlements.
propositions.quote: Picketing is . . . part of a group of economic sanctions which are considered key to the scheme of collective bargaining as a whole

paragraphs.summary: The court describes picketing as a historically crucial economic sanction in collective bargaining.

propositions.text: Public opinion often determines labour dispute outcomes.
propositions.quote: it is often the weight of public opinion which will determine the outcome of the dispute

propositions.text: Unions may pressure public not to cross picketlines to resolve disputes.
propositions.quote: The imposition of public or economic pressure has come to be accepted as a legitimate price to pay to encourage the parties to resolve their dispute.

propositions.text: Strikes are not peaceful events; pressure is permissible if not tortious or criminal.
propositions.quote: strikes are not tea parties: para. 90. This Court has acknowledged that such pressure is permissible as long as it does not rise to the level of a tortious or criminal act

paragraphs.summary: The court explains public opinion and pressure are legitimate in labour disputes if lawful.

propositions.text: PIPA restricts union communication and persuasion during lawful strikes, impairing bargaining strategies.
propositions.quote: PIPA imposes restrictions on a union’s ability to communicate and persuade the public of its cause, impairing its ability to use one of its most effective bargaining strategies in the course of a lawful strike.

propositions.text: PIPA's infringement on freedom of expression is disproportionate to its objective in this case.
propositions.quote: this infringement of the right to freedom of expression is disproportionate to the government’s objective of providing individuals with control over personal information

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PIPA disproportionately infringes union freedom of expression during lawful strikes.

propositions.text: Not all union activities are condoned, but PIPA's broad restrictions violate s. 2(b) and are unjustified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: To the extent that PIPA restricted the Union’s collection, use and disclosure of personal information for legitimate labour relations purposes, the Act violates s. 2 (b) of the Charter and cannot be justified under s. 1 .

propositions.text: Freedom of expression and privacy are not absolute; balance must consider nature of privacy and expression.
propositions.quote: freedom of expression is not an absolute value and both the nature of the privacy interests implicated and the nature of the expression must be considered in striking an appropriate balance.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds PIPA's broad restrictions violate freedom of expression and cannot be justified, emphasizing balance.

propositions.text: PIPA and its regulation violate s. 2(b) by restricting union use of personal information during lawful strikes.
propositions.quote: Do the Personal Information Protection Act...violate s. 2 (b)...insofar as they restrict a union’s ability to collect, use or disclose personal information during the course of a lawful strike? Answer: Yes.

propositions.text: The infringement is not a reasonable limit under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: If so, is the infringement a reasonable limit prescribed by law...under s. 1...Answer: No.

paragraphs.summary: The court answers yes to s. 2(b) violation and no to justification under s. 1 for PIPA's restrictions.

propositions.text: The Commissioner and Attorney General prefer PIPA be struck down entirely if unsuccessful.
propositions.quote: Both the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta and the Attorney General of Alberta stated...they would prefer that PIPA be struck down in its entirety.

propositions.text: Given PIPA's integrated structure, it is inappropriate to pick and choose amendments; it should be struck down entirely.
propositions.quote: Given the comprehensive and integrated structure of the statute, we do not think it is appropriate to pick and choose among the various amendments that would make PIPA constitutionally compliant

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees PIPA should be struck down entirely due to its integrated structure.

propositions.text: Declare PIPA invalid but suspend invalidity for 12 months for legislature to fix constitutionality
propositions.quote: We would therefore declare PIPA to be invalid but suspend the declaration of invalidity for a period of 12 months to give the legislature time to decide how best to make the legislation constitutional.

propositions.text: Quash the Adjudicator’s order instead of sustaining Court of Appeal's constitutional exemption
propositions.quote: Rather than sustain the constitutional exemption ordered by the Court of Appeal, we would simply quash the Adjudicator’s order.

paragraphs.summary: The Court declares PIPA invalid but suspends invalidity for 12 months and quashes the Adjudicator's order instead of sustaining the Court of Appeal's exemption.

propositions.text: The Union is entitled to costs and appeal is substantially dismissed with costs
propositions.quote: The Union is entitled to its costs. Appeal substantially dismissed with costs.

propositions.text: Lists solicitors for appellant, respondent, and various interveners with their locations
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta: Jensen Shawa Solomon Duguid Hawkes, Calgary. Solicitor for the appellant the Attorney General of Alberta: Attorney General of Alberta, Edmonton. Solicitors for the respondent: Chivers Carpenter, Edmonton. Solicitor for the intervener the Attorney General of Canada: Attorney General of Canada, Toronto. Solicitor for the intervener the Attorney General of Ontario: Attorney General of Ontario, Toronto. Solicitors for the intervener the Privacy Commissioner of Canada: Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt, Toronto; Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Ottawa. Solicitors for the intervener the Canadian Civil Liberties Association: Torys, Toronto. Solicitors for the intervener the British Columbia Civil Liberties Association: Moore, Edgar, Lyster, Vancouver. Solicitor for the intervener the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario: Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, Toronto. Solicitors for the interveners the Coalition of British Columbia Businesses and Merit Canada: Heenan Blaikie, Ottawa. Solicitors for the intervener the Information and Privacy Commissioner of British Columbia: Lovett Westmacott, Vancouver. Solicitors for the intervener the Alberta Federation of Labour: Chivers Carpenter, Edmonton.

paragraphs.summary: The Court orders costs to the Union and substantially dismisses the appeal, then lists solicitors for all parties and interveners.
